summary: Describes how OSPF can be used between customer edge and provider edge routers in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs. BGP carries the customer's routes across the provider backbone, and this document explains how they interact with the customer's OSPF routing. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A customer's network talks to the phone company's network using one routing language. This explains how that language works between them so offices across the country feel like one network.

subtitle: How a provider's edge router can speak OSPF to a customer's router while BGP carries the routes between sites.

tldr.problem: The base BGP/MPLS IP VPN specification assumes BGP on the link between provider and customer routers, but many customers already run OSPF and want to keep it, without VPN routes showing up as AS-external routes.
tldr.mechanism: Provider edge routers run a separate OSPF instance per customer domain, carry OSPF details across the backbone as BGP extended communities, and hand routes back to the customer as inter-area (type 3) LSAs. Optional sham links make the backbone look like an intra-area link.
tldr.outcome: A customer can swap a private OSPF backbone for a VPN service with little change to its own routers. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 4364.

today: RFC 4577 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4364. The metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It companions RFC 4576, which defines the DN bit used for loop prevention.

sections.title: OSPF on the PE/CE Link
sections.content:
RFC 4364 (referred to as [VPN]) describes how a service provider uses its IP backbone to offer a VPN service. A customer's edge devices (CE) connect to the provider's edge routers (PE). The PE routers of one VPN use BGP to distribute that VPN's routes to each other, and CE routers at different sites do not peer with each other. The base specification presumes BGP between PE and CE. RFC 4577 allows OSPF there instead, and it updates RFC 4364.

The RFC lists the trade-offs. The disadvantage is that the provider's PE router gets involved, however peripherally, in a customer site's IGP. The advantages are that CE administrators need no expertise in any other routing protocol, CE routers need no other protocol, and customers moving off a traditional OSPF backbone have an easier transition. No special procedures are needed in the CE router: it just runs whatever OSPF it already has. All the new rules apply to the PE.
sections.eli5: If the office already speaks one language, it is easier to let the phone company learn that language than to make every office learn a new one.

sections.title: What the Design Has to Achieve
sections.content:
Sites are in the same OSPF domain if routes between them should count as intra-network routes. With the ordinary BGP/OSPF interaction rules, routes from another site would arrive as type 5 LSAs (AS-external routes) and could not be told apart from truly external routes. So PEs need a modified procedure that aims for these requirements:

  • Make no assumption about the OSPF topology: sites need not be stub or NSSA sites, and may have one area or several.
  • Present routes between sites in the same domain as inter-area routes in type 3 LSAs, which also allows an "OSPF backdoor link" between two sites.
  • Allow a backdoor link even when both sites are in the same area and neither attached router is an area 0 router.
  • Let CE routers act as area 0 routers, even when the backbone is several segments joined only by the VPN service.
  • Make transition from a legacy private backbone simple, with metrics adjustable so OSPF prefers the VPN backbone.
  • Carry the OSPF metric transparently across the VPN backbone.

Routes from sites not in the same OSPF domain appear as AS-external routes.
sections.eli5: The offices want the route through the phone company to look like a regular hallway inside the building, not like a road to a different city.

sections.title: VRFs, OSPF Instances and Area 0
sections.content:
A PE that attaches to more than one OSPF domain MUST run an independent OSPF instance for each domain, and the instance serving as the provider's own IGP must be separate from all of them. Each PE/CE interface belongs to no more than one instance, and each instance is associated with a single VRF (the per-site routing and forwarding table from RFC 4364).

OSPF-learned routes are installed in the VRF and may be exported into BGP as VPN-IPv4 routes. At other PEs, a VPN-IPv4 route that matches an import Route Target and wins the BGP decision process is installed in the VRF, and may then be redistributed into the attached OSPF instances. If a VRF has both an OSPF route and a BGP route for the same prefix, the OSPF route is preferred. The one exception is when the OSPF route's next hop is a sham link.

Each PE/CE link is assigned by configuration to any OSPF area, including area 0. A PE with a link in a non-zero area acts as an Area Border Router for it, and PEs are considered area 0 routers. If the domain has area 0 routers other than PEs, at least one of them MUST be a CE router with an area 0 link, possibly a virtual link, to at least one PE. The VPN backbone can then act as a higher level of hierarchy above area 0, so a legacy backbone may be disconnected during a transition.
sections.eli5: The phone company keeps a separate notebook for each customer, so one customer's directions never get mixed up with another's.

sections.title: Preventing Routing Loops
sections.content:
A route sent to a CE must never come back into BGP through another PE. A PE therefore MUST set the DN bit in the options field of every type 3 LSA it sends to a CE, and also in the type 5 LSAs it generates for routes from outside the CE's domain. Any LSA that arrives from a CE with the DN bit set MUST NOT be used in the route calculation.

Some deployed implementations never set the DN bit and use an OSPF route tag instead. For backward compatibility, implementations MUST by default support the VPN Route Tag: type 5 LSAs the PE originates carry it, and a type 5 LSA received from a CE with that tag MUST NOT be used. Its use may be disabled by configuration when no longer needed. Its value must be configurable and distinct from other tags in the domain. For a two-byte AS number the default SHOULD be derived from it, and for a four-byte AS number a value MUST be configured.

The RFC warns that these steps do not remove all loop sources. If a route is redistributed from OSPF into another protocol such as RIP, where the loop-prevention information is lost, and back again, a loop could occur. So extreme care is needed with mutual redistribution between the OSPF domain and any third routing domain.
sections.eli5: Every route handed out by the phone company gets a stamp saying "already seen". If it ever comes back with the stamp, it is thrown away so it cannot go round in circles.

sections.title: OSPF Details Carried in BGP
sections.content:
For every prefix that OSPF installed in the VRF, the PE creates a VPN-IPv4 route in BGP with extra extended communities attributes so the route can be turned back into an OSPF route "transparently", as if BGP had not been involved:

  • OSPF Domain Identifier (type 0005, 0105 or 0205; type 8005 MAY be used for backward compatibility): an eight-byte value that says which OSPF domain a route came from. It MUST be present when the instance has a non-NULL primary Domain Identifier. Two instances are in the same domain when both use the NULL identifier, or each has the other's primary identifier.
  • OSPF Route Type (type 0306): MUST be present. It holds a 4-byte area number, a 1-byte route type and a 1-byte options field.
  • OSPF Router ID (type 0107): OPTIONAL, carrying the Router ID of the PE that installed the route.
  • MED: by default SHOULD be set to the OSPF distance plus 1.

Routes a PE receives in type 4 LSAs MUST NOT be redistributed to BGP. The Site of Origin attribute is OPTIONAL for OSPF-learned routes, which trades extra overhead against automatic repair of a partitioned site.

For IANA, the RFC assigns the BGP Extended Communities types 0005, 0105 and 0205 for the Domain Identifier, 0306 for the Route Type and 0107 for the Router ID, all in the first-come first-served range.
sections.eli5: When directions travel through the phone company, a small label is attached saying which office they came from and what kind of road it was, so the other office can read them as if nothing happened in between.

sections.title: Sham Links
sections.content:
Suppose two sites in the same area are both attached to different PEs and also joined by a direct backdoor link. By default the route through the backbone looks inter-area, so OSPF prefers the intra-area backdoor link. To make OSPF prefer the backbone, the route through it has to look intra-area. A sham link does this by making it appear that an intra-area link joins the two PE routers. Support for sham links is OPTIONAL.

  • Each VRF has a configurable 32-bit Sham Link Endpoint Address in the VPN's address space. It MUST be distributed by BGP as a VPN-IPv4 prefix 32 bits long and MUST NOT be advertised by OSPF.
  • Sham links are manually configured at both ends, and may exist in any area including area 0. A sham link is up only if a route to the remote endpoint address is installed in the VRF.
  • OSPF packets on a sham link use the endpoint addresses as IP source and destination. Sham links SHOULD be treated as OSPF demand circuits, so LSAs are flooded without periodic refresh.
  • The sham link is an unnumbered point-to-point link advertised as a type 1 link in a type 1 LSA. Its metric MUST be configurable, and the defaults are a Hello Interval of 10 seconds and a Router Dead Interval of 40 seconds.
  • A packet whose best route uses the sham link MUST be forwarded according to the corresponding BGP route, as MUST packets addressed to the remote endpoint.
sections.eli5: A sham link is a pretend hallway drawn on the map so the route through the phone company looks like a hallway inside the building and can be preferred over a back door.

sections.title: Handing BGP Routes Back to the Customer
sections.content:
Only routes installed in the VRF and used for forwarding are redistributed into OSPF, and the configuration may further limit them, for example to a default route only. How a route is advertised depends on its domain and its original type.

  • External routes: if the route type says external, or the route comes from a different domain (or no OSPF domain), it is advertised in a type 5 LSA, or in a type 7 LSA if the PE/CE link is in an NSSA. The DN bit MUST be set, and the VPN Route Tag MUST be included unless disabled. By default a type 2 metric is used, taken from the MED. The forwarding address is 0.
  • Summary routes: if the route is in the same domain, it is reported in a type 3 LSA, even if its area number matches the CE's area. A partitioned area connected only through the VPN therefore appears as two areas with inter-area routes between them.
  • NSSA routes are treated like external routes.

This makes every PE appear to be an ASBR attached to all external routes, so a multihomed site can get several type 5 LSAs with the same information.
sections.eli5: Routes from the same company come back looking like normal paths between its own offices. Routes from outsiders come back marked as coming from outside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC covers only what is specific to OSPF as the PE/CE protocol. A PE may run OSPF as the provider's IGP and as the IGP of one or more VPNs, which is why independent instances are required: routes must not leak between the backbone and a VPN, or between VPNs.

OSPF cryptographic authentication SHOULD be used between PE and CE and MUST be implemented on each PE. Without it, a CE might not really belong to the VPN that the PE assigns it to. An attacker could also insert spoofed messages in either direction. Spoofed messages to the CE could compromise routing at its site, and spoofed messages to the PE could cause improper VPN routing or a denial of service on the VPN.
sections.eli5: The two routers should check each other's password, so a stranger cannot pretend to be one of them and send everyone the wrong way.

data.title: Value field of the OSPF Route Type attribute

fields.name: Area Number
fields.desc: 32-bit area number. 0 for AS-external routes; non-zero means internal to the domain and within that area.

fields.name: Route Type
fields.desc: Kind of OSPF route; see the table of values.

fields.name: Options
fields.desc: Used only for route types 5 and 7; the least significant bit set means a type 2 metric.

items.label: Intra-area
items.desc: Route came from a type 1 or type 2 LSA.

items.label: Inter-area
items.desc: Route came from a type 3 LSA.

items.label: External
items.desc: AS-external route; the area number must be 0.
